passage:
First week: Farida got into the Hyderabad data-science internship and told everyone it was luck. "They probably mixed up my file." She stayed at the office till ten every night, checking every line of code twice.
Third week: Her mentor praised her dashboard in the team meeting. Farida's face went hot. "Oh, anyone could have done that," she said, and worked straight through lunch. That night she lay awake, sure someone would soon find out.
Fifth week: At the interns' chai break, she finally said it aloud to Nirmala: "I keep thinking I'm a fraud here." Nirmala put her cup down. "Seriously? Me too. Every day." Two others at the table nodded. Farida laughed for the first time in weeks, and that evening she left at six.

qa.q: How late did Farida stay at the office in the first week?
qa.a: She stayed at the office till ten every night.

qa.q: What was Farida afraid of as she lay awake in the third week?
qa.a: She was afraid someone would soon find out she didn't deserve her place.

qa.q: What turning point came in the fifth week, and why did it help?
qa.a: Farida named the feeling aloud to Nirmala and learned that others felt the same, which eased the fear and let her leave at six.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when Farida admitted feeling like a fraud?
qa.a: She seemed relieved to hear it too, since she felt the same every day.

grounding: A capable intern calls her success luck, brushes off praise and overworks, until naming the feeling to peers shows they share it.

passage: Zeenat, sit down. You think your Vidya ma'am was born confident? At twenty-two I joined this very bank as the only woman in the loans section, and I was sure they had hired me by mistake. When the manager praised my report, I said, "Oh, the clerk helped." He hadn't. I came in on Sundays to recheck files nobody had asked me to check. Then one day in the canteen I blurted out to the other new officers, "Do you ever feel you're just pretending?" Mohan, the cleverest of us, went red and said, "Every single day." We laughed so hard the tea spilled. After that, I stopped saying "the clerk helped".

qa.q: Who did Vidya credit when the manager praised the report?
qa.a: Vidya said the clerk had helped, though he hadn't.

qa.q: What was Vidya afraid of when she first joined the bank?
qa.a: She was afraid they had hired her by mistake and that she did not really belong.

qa.q: What turning point helped Vidya stop brushing off praise?
qa.a: She asked the other new officers if they felt they were pretending, and Mohan admitted he felt it every day, which showed her she wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt when Vidya asked her question in the canteen?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed but relieved, going red before admitting he felt the same.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls feeling like a fraud as a new officer, discounting praise and overworking, until sharing it with peers showed they felt it too.

passage: When Hiroshi's name went up on the dean's list at the university in Melbourne, his first thought was: someone made a mistake. He'd got the scholarship because the other applicants had bad days, he told himself; he'd passed Thermodynamics because the exam was easy that year. So he stayed in the library until it closed, every night, rewriting notes he already knew. When his tutor praised his design report, he said, "I just followed the template." One night Lindiwe, from his study group, found him there at eleven. "Can I tell you something embarrassing? I keep waiting for them to take my place back." Hiroshi stared at her. "You too?" They talked until the guard switched off the lights.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi say when his tutor praised his report?
qa.a: "I just followed the template."

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when his name went up on the dean's list?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and afraid, sure it was a mistake and that his success was just luck.

qa.q: What helped Hiroshi feel less alone with the fear?
qa.a: Lindiwe naming the same feeling, which showed him others feel it too.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Hiroshi says "You too?"
qa.a: Lindiwe probably feels relieved and less embarrassed, finding that someone she respects has the same fear.

grounding: Shows a capable student who calls his success luck, overworks and discounts praise until a peer shares the same fear.

passage: In his third week at the insurance office in Guwahati, Bhupen's manager said in the team meeting, "Bhupen's claims summary is the clearest we've had in months." Bhupen felt his face go hot, not with pride but with dread. Surely someone would check it properly and find the mistakes. He stayed till nine that night, re-checking every figure. At the tea counter next morning, Arnab, who'd joined the same month, said, "Nice work yesterday." "Luck," Bhupen said. "Honestly, I feel like a fraud here." Arnab laughed, not unkindly. "I've been looking up basic terms on my phone under the desk for three weeks." Bhupen laughed too, and something in his chest loosened.

qa.q: How late did Bhupen stay that night?
qa.a: Till nine.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when the manager praised him?
qa.a: He felt dread rather than pride, afraid someone would find mistakes and see him as a fraud.

qa.q: Which step helped Bhupen, and why?
qa.a: Admitting the fraud feeling to Arnab, because Arnab's reply showed a new colleague feels the same.

qa.q: What might Arnab be feeling when he admits to looking up terms under the desk?
qa.a: Arnab seems relieved to share his own worry, and kind in easing Bhupen's.

grounding: Illustrates a new employee who treats praise as luck, over-checks his work and finds relief when a peer shares the feeling.

passage:
Dear Rukmini-ma'am,
You were the first person who told me I could be an architect, so I thought I'd tell you I've made it, sort of. I got the job at the firm in Pune. Everyone here seems to know things I don't. When the senior partner liked my sketch for the school library, I told her it was mostly the team's idea, which it wasn't. I work late every day, sure that one day someone will notice I don't belong. Last Friday, at a chai break, I said this out loud to two other juniors. One said, "Wait, I thought it was only me." The other said she'd felt that way for a year. I laughed for the first time in weeks.
Sumit

qa.q: Which sketch did the senior partner like?
qa.a: The sketch for the school library.

qa.q: What is Sumit afraid of while working late every day?
qa.a: Sumit fears someone will notice Sumit doesn't belong, treating success as undeserved.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that helped?
qa.a: Said the feeling out loud to two other juniors at a chai break, and learned they felt it too.

qa.q: How might Rukmini-ma'am feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud of Sumit's job and touched to hear about the struggle honestly.

grounding: Shows a new professional who discounts praise, overworks and feels better after naming the feeling to peers.

passage:
Sachin, can I tell you something weird? When I got into the design programme, I was sure they'd made a mistake. I'm Gurleen, the one whose portfolio got picked for the first-week display, and I still thought, any day now someone will notice I don't belong.
When Professor Nair praised my poster, I said, "Oh, I just got lucky with the colours." Then I stayed in the studio till two a.m. every night, redoing things nobody asked me to redo.
Last Friday, at the peer circle, I finally said it out loud: "I feel like a fraud here." I expected everyone to go quiet. Instead Meher said, "Same." Then Arvind said, "Me too, every single day."
Half the room had the same fear. It didn't disappear. But it got smaller, and I went home at eight that night.

qa.q: What did Gurleen say when Professor Nair praised the poster?
qa.a: "Oh, I just got lucky with the colours."

qa.q: What was Gurleen afraid of after getting into the programme?
qa.a: Gurleen feared being found out as not belonging, sure the programme had made a mistake.

qa.q: What helped Gurleen's fear get smaller?
qa.a: Naming the feeling aloud at the peer circle and hearing Meher and Arvind say they felt the same, which let Gurleen go home at eight.

qa.q: How might Meher and Arvind have felt when Gurleen spoke up?
qa.a: They were probably relieved to hear someone else say it, since they shared the same fear and had kept quiet about it too.

grounding: Shows a capable student who thinks success is luck, discounts praise and overworks, until naming the fear reveals peers feel the same.
